cards.explanation: The answer is seventy years. Daniel understood from the sacred books that this was the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet about the desolation of Jerusalem (Daniel 9:2). I think that number hit him hard. I've been stuck in the back of a junk drawer for a long stretch myself, friends, so I know a number like that means something when you're counting.

The answer is fasting with sackcloth and ashes. Daniel turns to the Lord God to seek Him "…by prayer and petition, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes." (Daniel 9:3) Sackcloth is rough cloth, the opposite of your comfiest sweater. I think a man dressed like that means business, friends. I bet he isn't treating this prayer as a quick stop on his way somewhere else.

The answer is False. Daniel says "we," and that "we" includes him: "…we have sinned and done wrong. We have acted wickedly and rebelled." (Daniel 9:5) Later he says he was "…confessing my sin and that of my people Israel…" (Daniel 9:20). No dodging, friends, no "well, THEY did."

The word is prophets. Daniel confesses that they did not listen to God's servants the prophets, who spoke in His name to their kings, leaders, fathers, and all the people of the land (Daniel 9:6). Those messengers went from the top of the ladder all the way down, friends. And Daniel owns it with a plain "we."

The answer is compassion and forgiveness. Daniel says, "To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness, even though we have rebelled against Him" (Daniel 9:9). Notice, friends, that he doesn't wait for the rebelling to stop before he says it. Shame covers the people, and compassion and forgiveness still belong to God. That's a good thing to know about Him.

The word is Moses. Daniel says the oath and the curse are "…written in the Law of Moses the servant of God…" (Daniel 9:11). He says it again in verse 13: "Just as it is written in the Law of Moses…" Daniel keeps pointing to what was written, friends, and he doesn't argue with it.

The answer is False. Daniel says that after all this disaster, "…we have not sought the favor of the LORD our God by turning from our iniquities and giving attention to Your truth." (Daniel 9:13) He's telling it straight, friends, with no spin. The people hadn't turned, and Daniel says so.

The answer is Egypt. Daniel says God "…brought Your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand…" and made for Himself a name renowned to this day (Daniel 9:15). Daniel reaches back to something God already did. I think a man in a tight spot likes to remember that, friends.

The answer is False. Daniel says, "…we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion." (Daniel 9:18) He isn't handing God a list of things they did right, friends. He's leaning on God's compassion, and that's all.

The answer is True. Daniel prays, "For Your sake, O my God, do not delay…" (Daniel 9:19). It comes right after "O Lord, listen! O Lord, forgive! O Lord, hear and act!" He says it plainly, friends, and he means it.

The answer is Gabriel. Daniel calls him "…the man I had seen in the earlier vision…" and says he came "…in swift flight…" (Daniel 9:21). Daniel is still praying when he shows up. I think that's some pretty fast service, friends.

The answer is insight and understanding. Gabriel tells Daniel, "O Daniel, I have come now to give you insight and understanding." (Daniel 9:22) Daniel had already been reading and thinking about Jeremiah's word, friends. Now Gabriel comes to give him more, and he gets right to it.

The answer is True. Gabriel says, "At the beginning of your petitions, an answer went out, and I have come to tell you…" (Daniel 9:23). The answer went out at the beginning, friends, and Daniel was still praying when Gabriel arrived. The prayer had already been heard.

The answer is to put an end to sin. Gabriel says the seventy weeks are decreed "…to stop their transgression, to put an end to sin, to make atonement for iniquity…" (Daniel 9:24). It's right there in the middle of the list, friends. These are big things, and they're meant for Daniel's people and holy city.

The answer is True. Gabriel says the seventy weeks are decreed "…to bring in everlasting righteousness…" (Daniel 9:24). It sits in the same list as stopping transgression and making atonement, friends. Everlasting is a big word, and Gabriel uses it.

The word is distress. Gabriel says Jerusalem "…will be rebuilt with streets and a trench, but in times of distress." (Daniel 9:25) So the city gets rebuilt, friends, and the time around it is hard. Both parts are in the same sentence.

The answer is False. Gabriel says, "…until the end there will be war; desolations have been decreed." (Daniel 9:26) He doesn't promise peace until the end, friends. It's a heavy line, and he says it straight.

The answer is sacrifice and offering. Gabriel says, "…in the middle of the week he will put an end to sacrifice and offering." (Daniel 9:27) First he confirms a covenant with many for one week, friends, and then comes the middle of that week. It's a serious part of the message.
